newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rejects introduction of rabbit-control virus.
newsitem.headline: NZ rejects introduction of rabbit-control virus.

text.p: New Zealand will not permit rabbit calicivirus disease (RCD) to be imported into the country as a biological control for rabbits, the Ministry of Agriculture (MAF) said on Wednesday.

The decision comes after more than a year of discussions and submissions, following an official application by a group of farmers and local government organisations in June 1996 to import RCD as a means of controlling feral rabbits.

South Island farmers have clamoured for RCD's release in New Zealand since it escaped a quarantined trial in Australia in October 1995. They argued it offered a "once-in-a-lifetime chance" of beating New Zealand's rabbit problem.
Rabbits occupy around 56 percent of New Zealand's land area. They strip vegetation, erode soil through burrowing and have reduced some high country areas almost to moonscapes.

MAF deputy director-general Peter O'Hara said he empathised with farmers' sense of futility, as the benefits of achieving a good rabbit kill through expensive poisoning operations were often eroded by the prolificacy of remaining rabbits.
"I recognise that my decision will disappoint and even anger many people who are struggling to deal with rabbits using current technology," O'Hara said.
He said RCD was rejected because understanding was poor about the epidemiology of the virus and the disease it produced.
There was "significant uncertainty" over its effectiveness as a biocontrol agent, and nobody had yet come up with an adequate programme for its management.
O'Hara said it was not even known for sure how the disease was spread, or why its impact on Australian rabbit populations varied.

It was not possible to predict the behaviour of the disease in New Zealand or its indirect effects on indigenous plants and animals. Trialling RCD in New Zealand was not an option because of the difficulties of containing a virus, O'Hara said.

MAF would follow RCD's progress in Australia, and if the experience across the Tasman allowed more confidence that it could be manipulated to control rabbits, New Zealand might reconsider the question of its importation.

O'Hara said it was thought insects were responsible for carrying the virus to the Australian mainland from the quarantined project on Wardang Island, five kilometres off the South Australian coast. He said the risk of an accidental introduction of the virus to New Zealand was low.
"I really don't think that is a probability...but I cannot say with any certainty that an attempted illegal introduction would not succeed," he told journalists.
Screening at New Zealand's international airports was intensified after RCD escaped the Australian quarantine.

Twenty million rabbits are estimated to have died within three months of the virus infecting Australian rabbit populations. In September 1996 RCD was officially approved for use there, and has now spread through all parts of Australia.
Rabbits infected with RCD die from respiratory and heart failure within 40 hours and with no visible distress.
RCD has killed hundreds of millions of wild rabbits on four continents since it was first seen in domestic rabbits in China in 1984. A vaccine now exists to protect domestic rabbits.
